content: Perinatal stroke encompasses a range of cerebrovascular diseases that occur between 20 weeks of fetal development and 28 days after birth. Current acute treatment options for perinatal stroke are limited to supportive care, such as managing hypoglycemia and seizures. Stem cell-based therapies have emerged as a potential strategy to repair, restore, or regenerate damaged brain tissue. Preclinical research has led to ongoing studies in human neonates. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and risks of stem cell-based interventions for treating stroke in newborns, comparing them to either a control group (placebo or no treatment) or other types or sources of stem cell-based therapies. The review also aimed to evaluate different types of stem cells, such as mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs), mononuclear cells, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, neural stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells, or induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cells, as well as their sources (e.g., autologous or allogeneic, derived from bone marrow, cord blood, or other tissues). A comprehensive search was conducted in February 2023 across CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and three clinical trial registries. The review also planned to examine reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews to identify additional studies. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials, quasi-randomized controlled trials, and cluster trials that compared stem cell-based interventions to controls or to other types or sources of stem cells. All types of transplantation were considered, regardless of the cell source (e.g., bone marrow, cord blood, Wharton’s jelly, placenta, adipose tissue, peripheral blood), graft type (autologous or allogeneic), or dose. The primary outcomes of interest were all-cause neonatal mortality, major neurodevelopmental disability, and immune rejection or other serious adverse events. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality before hospital discharge, seizures, adverse effects, and death or major neurodevelopmental disability at 18 to 24 months of age. The GRADE approach was planned to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome. No completed or ongoing randomized trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. Three studies were excluded: two were phase 1 trials, and one involved newborns with conditions other than stroke (e.g., cerebral ischemia and anemia). Among the excluded studies, one phase 1 trial investigated the use of intranasal bone marrow-derived MSCs in term neonates diagnosed with perinatal arterial ischemic stroke (PAIS). This trial demonstrated that a single intranasal application was feasible and not associated with severe adverse events. However, the study included only 10 infants, and follow-up was limited to three months. Currently, there is no evidence available to evaluate the efficacy or safety of stem cell-based interventions for treating stroke in newborns. Future clinical trials should prioritize standardizing the timing, method of cell delivery, and cell processing to maximize therapeutic potential and ensure safety. Phase 1 studies and large animal models may provide a foundation for future randomized trials. Key outcome measures should include all-cause mortality, major neurodevelopmental disability, immune rejection, and other serious adverse events.
